overview.description: Bisca is Portugal's national trick-taking game, a close cousin of Italian Briscola and Spanish Brisca, sharing the same A-7-K-J-Q ranking. Played with a 40-card Portuguese deck, it features a fixed trump suit revealed by turning a card after the deal, a draw-down-to-empty mechanic, and point-count scoring (61+ out of 120 card points wins). Its elegant simplicity masks rich defensive and offensive play.

history.origins: Directly descended from the Italian game Briscola, carried to Portugal via trade and cultural exchange. Documented in Portuguese card-game literature from the 18th century onwards.
timeline: 1600s-1700s: Briscola spreads from Italy throughout the Iberian Peninsula.
1800s: Distinct Bisca rules solidify in Portugal (notably, the 7 not the 3 scores as the second trump).
Present: Remains one of the most popular card games in Portugal and among Portuguese diaspora. The 4-player team version (Sueca) is equally famous.
history.evolution: Bisca spawned Sueca (the 10-card partnership variant) which is arguably even more popular in Portugal today.
history.cultural: Part of everyday Portuguese social life; played in cafes, at family gatherings, and increasingly online.

setup.deck: 40 cards: A, 7, K, J, Q, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 in each suit. Remove 8s, 9s, and 10s from a standard deck.
setup.dealing: Deal 3 cards to each player (or more in variants). Turn the next card face-upâ€”this card's suit is Trump. Place the remaining deck crosswise on top of the trump-indicator card.

rules.objective: Win the deal by capturing 61 or more of the 120 card points in tricks. The pack has 120 points in total; the player or team with the majority (61+) wins. Often a match is played as best of seven games.
rules.gameplay: Phase 1 (Draw Phase): 1. Non-dealer leads. 2. No obligation to follow suitâ€”play any card. 3. Trick is won by highest trump, or highest of led suit if no trump. 4. Winner takes trick, draws a card from stock. Loser draws next. 5. Winner leads next trick. Phase 2 (Final Phase): When stock is empty, players play out remaining cards with normal trick-taking rules.
keyRules: There is NO obligation to follow suit during the draw phase.
Trump cards always beat non-trump cards.
The trump-indicator card is the last card drawn from the stock (taken by the winner of the last draw-phase trick).

strategy.basic: Hoard Aces and 7s. Lead low worthless cards to bait opponents into playing Aces.
strategy.intermediate: Trump Management: Don't waste Aces or 7s trumping low cards. Save trumps to beat opponent's Aces of side suits.
strategy.advanced: Stock Counting: As the deck depletes, track what's left. If you know the Ace of Hearts is unplayed, lead a heart to pull it out.
tips: The 7 of Trumps is worth 10 pointsâ€”protect it as fiercely as an Ace.
In 2-player, leading a '0-point' card forces the opponent to either waste a high card or let you win the trick.

difficulty.easy: Leads randomly. Plays Ace whenever possible.
difficulty.medium: Saves Aces. Counts trump remaining. Avoids trumping low-point tricks.
difficulty.hard: Tracks every card. Calculates exact point differential. Adjusts aggression based on stock size and current point totals.

customActions.description: Deal 3 cards to each player. Turn the next card face up as trump indicator. Stack the remaining deck crosswise on top of the trump card.
customActions.constraints: Dealer only; performed once at start of deal phase.

customActions.description: Play any card to the trick. No requirement to follow suit or trump. Trick is won by the highest trump in it, or if no trumps by the highest card of the suit led.
customActions.constraints: Legal when it is your turn to play in the draw or final phase.

customActions.description: Winner of the trick draws the top card from the stock first (without showing it); the loser draws the next. Known as biscar. When stock is empty, no more drawing.
customActions.constraints: After each trick during draw phase, winner draws first then loser; order may vary with more than two players (e.g. counter-clockwise from winner).

engine.handRankingSystem: Not applicable: Bisca scores individual card points in tricks rather than using poker-style hand rankings.
engine.deckDescription: One standard 40-card deck: ten ranks (ace through seven plus face cards) in each of four suits. No jokers; used for Bisca (a Portuguese point-trick game) with card-point scoring and a fixed trump suit.
engine.suitDescription: Four French suits (clubs, diamonds, hearts, spades). One suit is chosen as trump by turning a card after the deal; trump cards outrank non-trumps but card point values are identical across suits.
engine.rankDescription: Ten ranks per suit in the Iberian tradition (ace, two through seven, then face cards). Point values: aces and threes high, then kings, etc. Trick and trump order follow the 40-card pack rules for Bisca.

hero.tagline: The Ace is King. The Seven is Queen. Play wisely.

synthesis.shortDescription: Portugal's beloved national card game. Simple enough for a first lesson, deep enough for a lifetime. Capture Aces and Sevens; reach 61 points first.

prompts.human: Your opponent leads the King of Spades (4 pts). You have the Ace of Spades (11 pts) and the 7 of Hearts (trump, 10 pts). Win it cheaply with the Aceâ€”don't waste a trump on a measly King when the pot is small.
prompts.ai: Game: Bisca. Type: Ace-Ten/Draw. Ranking: A(11)>7(10)>K(4)>J(3)>Q(2)>others(0). No follow-suit in draw phase. Target: 61 points.

scoring.description: Count card points in won tricks.
scoring.winCondition: First to 61 card points wins the deal. Alternatively, best of 7 deals ('Partida').
scoring.splitRules: Tie (60-60) = no one wins the deal; play continues.
